latin.1996: THESIS I. INter ea quae sunt in Scholis excogitata ad conciliandam libertatem humanam cum certitudine & immutabilitate decretorum divinorum circa actus humanos, increbuit in primis scientia illa conditionata, ex qua rationem istius conciliationis petendam esse censuerunt Ludovicus Molina & Fonseca Jesuitae primi, & post eos plurimi, tum in Schola Romana, tum inter ipsos Protestantes. Itaque, Deo favente, de concordia Libertatis humanae cum decretis divinis acturi, & varia Doctorum placita ea de re exposituri, ab illa scientia initium sumendum nobis esse merito duximus.
latin.1997: II. Igitur maxima pars Doctorum Scholae Romanae in ea est sententia, Deum non solum praescire ea quae libere & contingenter quidem, sed tamen simpliciter & absolute futura sunt; verum etiam illa quae, licet nunquam futura sint, libere tamen eventura essent, posita hac, aut illa conditione. Exempli causa, Deum non tantum cognoscere quid singuli facturi sumus ad finem usque vitae, in variis illis statibus in quibus, ex certa Dei Providentia sumus collocandi; sed praeterea quid facturi essemus, si plane diversus esset futurus rerum status, & aliae atque aliae agendi occasiones sese nobis offerrent.
latin.1998: III. Porro, cum praescientia eorum quae sunt absolute futura, necessario sequatur decretum aliquod divinae voluntatis, quo statuerit haec & illa agentia creare, & in hoc, vel illo rerum ordine constituere, atque cum illis, prout necesse est, ad agendum concurrere; hanc scientiam eorum quae simpliciter futura non sunt, sed ex hypothesi tantum futura essent, volunt in Deo praecedere liberum omne voluntatis decretum. Nempe juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, Deum, priusquam ullum de re quacunque decretum condiderit, certo & distincte novisse quid creatura quaelibet possibilis libere factura sit, si voluerit Deus illam creare, & concursum suum illi non denegare, atque haec & illa objecta, sub circumstantiis istis & illis ei proponere.
latin.1999: IV. Quanquam autem ista scientia liberum quodvis decretum in Deo antecedat; nihilominus, ut patet ex dictis, in conditione sub qua res futura dicitur, includitur decretum, non quidem quod actu Deo inesse concipiatur, sed quod necessario in Deo ponendum esset ad hoc, ut res illa esse posset. Ac proinde conditionata illa futuritio, quae scientiae hujus objectum est, non desinit a quodam Dei decreto pendere: Verum non a decreto jam facto, sed quod faciendum a Deo supponitur, ut res illa vere futura dici possit. Nimirum more nostro Deus concipitur sic apud se cogitans, Si decernerem hunc Angelum, vel hominem creare, & concursum meum illi non subtrahere, in tali rerum dispositione hoc ageret, & non aliud; quanquam posset aliter agere.
latin.2000: V. Id observat Gabriel Vasquez in primam partem Thomae, Nihilominus, inquit, dicendum est ita Deum certo cognoscere futura sub conditione, ut etiam sub conditione subintelligatur Dei decretum de concurrendo cum arbitrio, hoc modo, Deus bene novit, si Petro in hac occasione, vel illa, darem hanc, vel illam vocationem, & ego cum illa cooperarer, secundum quod illa postularet, nec miraculose subtraherem concursum meum, fieret tale opus: possem tamen subtrahere, si placeret: utrum autem Deus esset negaturus concursum, an concessurus, in eo casu nihil decrevit ipse. Tom. 1. disput. 67. cap. 4.
latin.2001: VI. Nec absimilia sunt quae leguntur apud Franciscum Suaresium. Adde praeterea, inquit, simpliciter totum hunc effectum pendere a voluntate Dei, ut absolute sit, vel non sit, & consequenter etiam in illis conditionatis debere in antecedente includi voluntatem divinam, scilicet, si ipsa velit talem effectum, vel saltem velit illum permittere, & ad illum concurrere; & hoc modo etiam illa scientia habet habitudinem ad voluntatem divinam sub praedicta conditione. Libro secundo de scientia quam habet Deus de futuris contingentibus sub conditione propositis, prius ratione quam de ipsa conditione aliquid decernat, capite sexto.
latin.2002: VII. Caeterum quemadmodum ad hoc, ut in tempore agant causae liberae, non putant necessarium esse, ut a Deo praemoveantur, & praedeterminentur ad hunc aut illum actum: ita quoque Dei decretum unde pendet sive absoluta, seu conditionata futuritio actuum liberorum, non putant esse decretum aliquod causas liberas praemovendi, & praedeterminandi; sed absque tali decreto, vel simpliciter posito, vel saltem supposito, Deum certo praenosse quicquid factura sunt agentia libera vel absolute, vel sub conditione. Nempe ad hoc, ut res fit & praevideatur futura, sufficere si ponamus, vel supponamus in Deo decretum de subministrando concursu, quem solum putant ad agendum necessarium, & qui talis est ex eorum mente, ut semper praesto sit liberis agentibus, nec illa ad agendum vel applicet, vel praedeterminet.
latin.2003: VIII. Porro hanc scientiam vocant scientiam Mediam, quoniam, juxta ipsos, medium tenet inter scientiam quae dicitur in Scholis scientia Visionis, & illam quae dicitur simplicis intelligentiae. Per scientiam autem visionis intelligunt notitiam illam qua Deus novit ea quae extra ipsum existunt in aliqua temporis differentia, nempe quae sunt praeterita, praesentia, vel futura. Quae omnia Deus ab aeterno tam clare, certo, & distincte cognoscit, ac si actu ipsi praesentia essent, non secus ac illa quae coram intuemur. Unde est quod dicitur scientia Visionis, ad similitudinem, scilicet, Visus corporei, quo res oculis objectas cernimus. Atque haec scientia dicitur quoque scientia libera, quia sequitur liberum decretum divinae voluntatis de rebus creandis atque conservandis, sine quo, ut nihil existere potest, ita quoque nihil potest videri praesens, vel praevideri futurum. Adeoque, si Deus nihil creare decrevisset, ejusmodi scientia Deo tribui non posset.
latin.2004: IX. Per scientiam vero simplicis intelligentiae significant eam qua Deus novit & intelligit omnia possibilia rerumque essentias & connexiones omnes, seu necessarias, sive quomodocunque possibiles. Atque haec scientia dicitur naturalis, non libera; quia praecedit, juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, omne Dei decretum de rebus faciendis: neque potuit in Deo non esse, quanquam nihil extra se creare voluisset.
latin.2005: X. Scientia autem quam Deo tribuunt contingenter futurorum sub aliqua conditione, media ab illis vocatur, quoniam nec omnino convenit cum scientia visionis, nec etiam, cum scientia simplicis intelligentiae, sed de utraque aliquid participat. Nec enim est de rebus mere possibilibus, & abstracta ab omni consideratione existentiae, qualis est scientia simplicis intelligentiae: neque etiam est de rebus absolute futuris in aliqua temporis differentia, ex decreto Dei; qualis est scientia Visionis: Sed partim refert scientiam liberam, quia est de rebus libere futuris, si modo conditio poneretur, & in libertate Dei situm est, ut conditio illa ponatur: partim scientiam naturalem, quia praecedit omne decretum Dei, & Deus ea carere non potuit, etiamsi non decrevisset mundum, aut aliquid creare.
latin.2006: XI. Nihilominus scientiam istam futurorum sub conditione nonnulli, non mediam, sed conditionatam simpliciter appellant, quoniam censent illam facile revocari posse, vel ad scientiam visionis, juxta quosdam; vel juxta plures alios, ad scientiam simplicis intelligentiae: quo de numero sunt Vasquez & Gregorius de Valentia. Quanquam observat Vasquez nihil obesse, si doctrinae & claritatis gratia, inter duas illas scientiae divinae species tertium aliquod membrum constituatur: atque hanc dissensionem vocum esse, non rerum, nec multum referre, si qui hac in re varie loquantur. Tom. 1. disp. 67. sub finem.
latin.2007: XII. Caeterum scientiam talem Deo convenire, qua certo praenoscat contingenter futura sub aliqua conditione, probari posse putant Scripturae testimoniis, & argumentis ex ratione ductis. Et primo quidem ex Scriptura proferunt varia exempla praedictionum de iis quae non contigerunt quidem, sed quae, positis his aut illis rebus, eventura erant: Quale est illud quod legitur 1 Sam. 23. v. 11, 12. Ubi quum David rogasset Dominum, An si in Urbe Kebela maneret, Saul venturus esset ad capiendum ipsum. Et si ille venisset, An Kebilitae ipsum tradituri essent in manum Saulis? responsum accepit & Saulem venturum, & Kebilitas ipsum in manum Saulis tradituros, si in urbe Kebila maneret. Ac proinde utrumque istud, quod a libera Saulis & Kehilitarum voluntate pendebat, certo praescivit Deus, sub conditione quae locum non habuit, David fugam arripiente, qua de causa neutrum revera factum est.
latin.2008: XIII. Simile est quod Deus interdicens Israelitis, ne filios, vel filias suas matrimonio jungerent cum filiabus vel filiis populorum a foedere Dei alienorum, hujus sui praecepti hanc rationem reddit, quod alioqui gentes illae exterae Israelitarum corda seducerent, & inclinarent ad Deos suos. Non ingrediemini ad eas, neque de illis ingredientur ad vestras: certissime enim avertent corda vestra ut sequamini Deos earum, 1 Reg. 11. 2. Unde patet, Deum certo praescivisse Israelitarum corda seductum iri, si illegitimis ejusmodi connubiis sese implicarent. Quod & in Salomone ob conditionem positam impletum est, in plerisque vero aliis Israelitis non item, propterea quod in illis locum non habuit illa conditio antecedens.
latin.2009: XIV. Ex novo quoque Testamento multum urgent Christi verba quae habentur Matth. 11. 21. Vae tibi Corazaim, vae tibi Bethsaida: quia si in Tyro & Sidone factae essent virtutes quae factae sunt in vobis, olim sacco & cinere poenitentiam egissent. Ubi affirmat Christus poenitentiam acturos fuisse Tyrios & Sidonios, si eadem media Deus erga illos adhibuisset, quibus erga Judaeos usus est. Adeoque Deus, illorum poenitentiam sub ista conditione futuram fuisse ab aeterno noverat. Ac vim quoque faciunt in eo quod Dominus in quodam Pauli raptu jubet eum ocyus Hierosolymis exire, propterea quod non essent testimonium de ipso suscepturi. Nempe praevidebat Deus, quod si Christum Paulus Judaeis praedicaret, non essent fidem ejus testimonio habituri, Act. 22. 18.
latin.2010: XV. Praeterea multis argumentis ex ratione ductis probari posse putant talem scientiam in Deo reperiri. Et primo quidem inde quod in propositionibus de futuro contingenti sub aliqua conditione determinata est veritas, vel falsitas, non minus quam in propositionibus de iis quae sunt absolute futura; ac proinde sunt illae quoque scientiae divinae objectum: quandoquidem nulla veritas latere potest intellectum infinitum, qualis divinus est. Propositiones autem de futuris contingentibus sub aliqua conditione determinate veras, vel falsas esse, ex eo conficitur quod inter eas vera potest esse contradictio, haud secus ac inter eas quae sunt de rebus absolute futuris. Siquidem prorsus haec sibi contradicunt, Si Petrus in talibus circumstantiis ponatur, peccabit, Et, Non si Petrus in talibus circumstantiis ponatur, peccabit. In omnibus autem contradictoriis, necesse est alteram partem contradictionis veram, alteram falsam esse.
latin.2011: XVI. Deinde si verum est, quod Petrus positus in talibus circumstantiis peccet, sane non solum antequam in iis poneretur, sed etiam antequam in iis ex decreto Dei ponendus esset, verum erat, quod si in iis poneretur, peccaret, adeoque Deus ante suum decretum novit istud sub tali conditione futurum fuisse. Et prius ratione quam verum sit aliquid absolute futurum, verum est illud fuisse futurum conditionate.
latin.2012: XVII. Praeterea sapientis est priusquam aliquid decernat, animo conceptum habere quid secuturum sit ex rebus a se decernendis, atque faciendis. Cum ergo Deus sapientissime omnia decreverit, necesse ut ratione prius quam decreverit hunc, aut illum creare, taliaque illi objicere, & hoc, vel illo modo cum eo concurrere, nosset quid esset ex istis omnibus consecuturum, & quid, iis positis, creatura libere factura, vel omissura esset, qua in cognitione consistit scientia conditionata, de qua quaestio est.
latin.2013: XVIII. Adde quod, nisi talem scientiam Deo tribuamus, infinitae poterunt quaestiones Deo proponi, ad modum illarum quas proposuit David, ad quas Deus nihil certum & perspicuum respondere poterit, nisi rem esse quae sciri non potest; quod non parum divinae omni scientiae detrahere videtur. Exempli gratia, quaerat aliquis, quid facturus fuisset iste, qui placida morte in Christo decessit, si oblatum ipsi fuisset martyrium? An si iste, vel ille talis puellae quae alteri nupsit, prior nuptias ambivisset, assensum fuisset impetraturus nec ne? si certus aliquis in regem Poloniae eligeretur, quomodo in illo regno sese gesturus esset? & infinita hujusmodi, de quibus cum homines sagaces, & rerum periti conjicere possint, non est verisimile ea simpliciter a Deo nesciri. Ac indignum Deo videtur, illum non certo compertum habere, quod homo probabili conjectura assequi potest. Quod si quis dicat, Deum talia quidem scire, & de iis distincte & perspicue respondere posse, sed talem scientiam praesupponere liberum decretum de rerum istarum futuritione, in hoc vel illo casu, inde sequetur in Deo esse infinita decreta de rebus nunquam revera futuris, ac proinde frustranea, inania, & otiosa quod valde absurdum est.
latin.2014: XIX. Veruntamen non pauci Doctores Scholae Romanae, & praesertim illi qui Thomistae recentiores dicuntur, praeter scientiam naturalem, quae dicitur scientia simplicis intelligentiae, & scientiam liberam, quae scientia visionis vocatur, negant in Deo dari scientiam ullam mediam, per quam scilicet, ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, Deus noverit ea quae nec simpliciter possibilia sunt, nec etiam sunt absolute futura, sed futura essent sub hac, vel illa conditione, & a creaturis intelligentibus hoc, vel illo dato libere fierent.
latin.2015: XX. Putant enim nihil esse ullo modo futurum, vel absolute, vel sub conditione, nisi virtute alicujus decreti, quod actu in Deo praecedat, & quo Deus constituerit id quod futurum dicitur, vel efficere, vel saltem permittere; adeoque ante decretum divinae voluntatis praedeterminantis voluntatem ad alteram partem contradictionis, vel contrarietatis, non esse scibile quid in particulari faciet homo, vel quid facturus esset, si constitueretur in talibus circumstantiis; sed solum quid posset facere: idque quoniam ante tale decretum, res nec est futura, neque non futura, sed mere possibilis, & indifferens ad hoc, ut futura sit, vel non futura sit.
latin.2016: XXI. Itaque non negant quidem quaedam contingenter & libere futura sub aliqua conditione a Deo certo praesciri, & in Scriptura praedici, quemadmodum Deus Davidi praedixit, quod si in urbe Kehila maneret Saul, venturus erat ad ipsum prehendendum; & rursus quod, si Saul ad urbem illam veniret, incolae erant ipsum in manus Saul tradituri: Sed pertendunt certam illam Dei praescientiam sequi liberum in Deo decretum, quo statuerit ut haec aut illa fiant, si adimpleatur haec vel illa conditio. Exempli causa, Deum praescivisse quod David manente in urbe Kehila, Saul venturus esset, & Kehilani essent Davidem tradituri, quia, posita illa conditione, Deus decreverat utrumque permittere, & ad substantiam illorum actuum voluntatem Saulis, & incolarum urbis Kehila praedeterminare. Prout latius videre est apud Didacum Alvarez de Auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 1. cap. 6. cujus Titulus est, Quod praeter scientiam mere naturalem, & mere liberam, nulla sit, etiam in Deo, scientia media constituenda. Et sequenti quoque capite, in quo Doctorum diversae sententiae objectiones dissolvit.
latin.2017: XXII. Quod spectat autem Protestantes, variae quoque sunt eorum hac de re sententiae. Et primo quidem illi qui in Belgio Remonstrantes vocantur, videntur communi consensu scientiam illam mediam qualis hactenus descripta est probare, & agnoscere Deum non solum quae sunt absolute futura praevidere, sed etiam quaecunque libere futura essent, in quocunque rerum ordine Deo placeret agentia libera collocare.
latin.2018: XXIII. Et primo quidem solennem a temporibus Molinae distinctionem triplicis in Deo scientiae, ut commodam refert Simon Episcopius. Observandum venit, inquit, triplicem Deo scientiam tribui solere. Unam, quae necessaria est, & practica, atq; simplicis intelligentiae dicitur, quae ex natura sua omni voluntatis liberae actu prior est, qua Deus seipsum & alia omnia possibilia intelligit. Alteram liberam, quae Visionis dicitur, & actu Voluntatis liberae posterior est, qua Deus omnia, quae facere, aut permittere decrevit eodem ordine novit quo ea decrevit facere, aut permittere ut fiant. Tertiam Mediam, qua Deus novit quid homines, aut Angeli pro sua libertate facturi essent, sub conditione, si cum his aut illis circumstantiis, in hoc vel in illo statu, aut ordine constituerentur. An haec divinae scientiae distinctio recte fiat, nos non expendimus. Quin ea commode & doctrinae gratia fieri possit, neutiquam dubitamus. Institutionum Theologicarum libro quarto, capite 19. De ordine & modo scientiae divinae.
latin.2019: XXIV. Nicolaus vero Grevinchovius prolixe pro hac scientia disputat in Responso quod opposuit Dissertationi de Redemptione generali, & Electione ex fide praevisa pag. 393. & seqq. Cujus Responsi examen instituit Guliel. Amesius in libro cui titulus est, Rescriptio Scholastica & brevis ad Nic. Grevinchovii Responsum. Et similiter Curcellaeus satis ostendit sibi probari scientiam illam Mediam seu conditionatam, quam in Scholis Deo tribuunt, dum in eo laudat Gomarum, quod ab Arminio edoctus, in posterioribus suis Thesibus, De Aeterno Dei decreto, & De Praedestinatione, Scientiam conditionatam in Deo agnovit; cujus ope, inquit, ingens illud ἄτοπον, quod Deum primi hominis peccati, & per consequens caeterorum omnium, quae ex eo fluere putantur, authorem faceret, a sua sententia amolitur. Praefatione praefixa libro cui titulus est Jacobi Arminii Examen Thesium Francisci Gomari de Praedestinatione.
latin.2020: XXV. Sed & inter Reformatos qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, reperiuntur nonnulli agnoscentes in Deo scientiam illam conditionatam, per quam ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, novit quid causa libera quaelibet, in quovis rerum ordine, pro ingenita sibi libertate, factura esset. Inter quos primum numerandus videtur Franciscus ille Gomarus, in hanc sententiam jam a Curcellaeo citatus. Etenim scribens in locum Matth. 11. v. 21. Postquam observavit Tyriorum Poenitentiam, posita miraculorum Christi conditione, futuram, intelligi hujusmodi, quae communis est Electis & Reprobis, credentibus & non credentibus: qualis, ex ejus mente, fuit Ninivitarum cum sacco Poenitentia; subjungit haec ipsa verba, Quod autem Christus de futura hac Tyriorum, posita illa conditione, poenitentia asserit, illius veritas ex indefinita divinae ipsius naturae praescientia constat, qua novit quidnam, quo posito antecedente, fuisset secuturum, etiamsi neutrum evenerit. Nam posita ea conditione, alterutrum fuisse eventurum, ut aut poenitentiam agerent, aut non agerent, omnibus notum est ex principio illo, quod duo opposita non possunt esse simul vera: sed utrum eorum fuisset futurum, cum res fuerit contingens, solus praevidit, qui infinita sua scientia omnia videt, nec solum necessaria, sed etiam futura contingentia certo praedicit. Similis locus est Ezech. 3. v. 6, 7. Ut refert Baldvinus Walaeus commentario suo in libros historicos Novi Testamenti ad locum Matthaei citatum.
latin.2021: XXVI. Robertus quoque Baronius expresse probat sententiam Fonsecae ponentis in Deo scientiam quandam conditionatam, ante liberum ipsius decretum, quae futurorum absolutam praescientiam antecedat. Deum, verbi causa, prius conditionate tantum scivisse quid eventurum esset, si Eva seducta a Serpente Adamum tentaret; postquam autem decrevit permittere ut Adamus obtemperaret uxori suae suadenti, non amplius conditionate, sed absolute praevidisse Adamum lapsurum.
latin.2022: XXVII. Atque sic suam & Fonsecae mentem ea de re declarat. Nempe Quemadmodum illi qui sapienter magnum aliquod opus moliuntur, prius apud se cogitant quid ex eo consequuturum sit, quam absolute & determinate illud facere decernant; ita Deum Opt. Max. more nostro intelligendi, priusquam absoluta determinataque voluntate vellet mundum condere, quasi apud se deliberantem cogitavisse quid esset secuturum, si coelum & terram, & ea omnia quae in iis continentur, hoc ipso modo & ordine quo actu ea postea disposuit, constitueret, & scientia quadam hypothetica scivisse qui & qualis eventus evenirent, si res omnes eo modo & ordine disponerentur, quo jam dispositae sunt: neque Deum scivisse tantum quid eveniret, si causae naturales hoc ordine ac modo quo dispositae sunt, constituerentur: sed etiam quid eveniret si causae liberae haberent has occasiones agendi, aut non agendi oblatas, quas jam habent, aut quas causae liberae quae prius existebant habuerunt: Deum enim, cujus judicia incomprehensibilia sunt, certo cognovisse quid esset eventurum, si hae aut illae occasiones hominibus, vel Angelis offerrentur: exempli causa, Deum per scientiam hanc conditionatam novisse quid esset eventurum, si Adami uxor seducta a Serpente Adamo suaderet ut pomum ederet. In Metaphysica generali ad Theologiae usum accommodata sect. 12. disp. 2. num. 55, & 56. & pluribus aliis locis in eadem disputatione.
latin.2023: XXVIII. Praesertim vero Antonius Walaeus in Academia Leydensi Professor agnoscit in Deo scientiam mediam, qua ex hypothesi res futurae cognoscuntur, etsi absolute futurae non sint, aut nondum sint. Et censet, verbi causa, Deum praescivisse Adamum sua libertate esse abusurum, si Deus eum talem conderet, donis ejusmodi ornaret, tentari permitteret, &c. & rem sic se habere de caeteris liberi arbitrii eventibus, ex Angelorum aut hominum arbitrio pendentibus. Atque hanc suam scientiam probat iis Scripturae locis quae supra citata sunt, & pluribus adhuc aliis, ut quod legitur Matthaei capite vigesimo quarto. Nisi abbreviati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salva ulla caro, Et si fieri posset seducerentur etiam electi, id est, nisi singulari gratia praeservarentur. Ex quibus & similibus locis manifestum esse dicit dari talem aliquam scientiam in Deo, ante omne decretum ejus, de eo quod certo futurum fuit. In locis communibus loco de scientia Dei, pag. 160. editionis in quarto.
latin.2024: XXIX. Ibidem vero monet non esse necessarium, ut haec scientia hypothetica statuatur tertia aliqua species scientiae; quia illa ad scientiam simplicis intelligentiae pertinet. Nam illud, inquit, est absolute necessarium, ut Deus omnes modos possibiles causarum secundarum, sive solae, sive cum aliis agant, ab aeterno conspexerit, ac proinde quid ex unaquaque certa hypothesi posita infallibiliter fieret, vel non fieret, si causas illas produceret, eas conservaret, & cum eis hoc aut illo modo concurreret, vel hoc aut illo modo disponeret, aut disponi sineret. Hoc nemo Christianus negabit.
latin.2025: XXX. Sed praecipue cavendum esse docet, nequis ista scientia abutatur vel ad decretum electionis a bono usu liberi Arbitrii hominis perpendendum, ut faciunt illi qui volunt, Deum priusquam hominem elegit, praevidisse quomodo, si haec aut illa gratia praeveniens & concomitans, in hoc aut illo ordine rerum, vel in hoc aut illo statu homini offerretur, ille per liberum arbitrium ei esset assensurus, aut non assensurus, adeo ut liberum arbitrium gratiam Dei eis determinet, non contra. Vel etiam ad negandam omnem Dei operationem efficacem in hominis convertendi voluntate, praeter moralem institutionem: quoniam, ut postea demonstraturum se confidit, Deus non tantum moraliter, sed etiam Physice agit in hominis voluntate, quando eum convertit.
latin.2026: XXXI. Atque hanc scientiam futurorum conditionatam, & quae liberum decretum praecedat, in Deo admittit quoque Paulus Ferrius Verbi divini apud Metenses Minister Celeberrimus, Praescivit, inquit, Deus sua quam conditionatam vocant scientia, hominem quocunque illum modo faceret, hoc vel illud effecturum; ac proinde lapsurum si labilem crearet & tentari sineret, & ipsum sibi ipsi committeret, pro innata sua ipsius libertate ad utrumque, & creaturae infirmitate: si autem laberetur, futurum ut omnes perirent, si vellet, vel aliquos inde posset eruere, ut ita in illis justitiam, in istis gratiam suam declararet, &c. Et postea rationem divinae Providentiae circa lapsum hominis exponens, Primo, inquit, Deus praevidit fore ut homo caderet, si crearetur labilis & tentaretur. Deinde (quia vidit expedire ita esse) placuit ipsi ut hoc fieret, non inferendo vim homini, sed hominem ita creando, tentationique & sibi permittendo. Quibus subjungit, paucis interjectis, Deum circa lapsum Hominis nihil statuisse, quin prius praevideret, praesupposita libertate & tentatione, fore ut infallibiliter laberetur. sections.title: Conditional knowledge, devised by Molina and Fonseca, is the starting point for reconciling freedom with God's decrees
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. Among those things which have been devised in the Schools to reconcile human liberty with the certainty and immutability of the divine decrees concerning human acts, that conditional knowledge has above all grown prevalent, from which Ludovicus Molina and Fonseca, Jesuits, first judged that the reason of that reconciliation must be sought, and after them very many, both in the Roman School, and among the Protestants themselves. Therefore, God favouring, being about to treat of the concord of human Liberty with the divine decrees, and to set forth the various opinions of the Doctors on that matter, we have deservedly judged that we must take our beginning from that knowledge.
pass_b: Of all the devices the schools have produced for reconciling human freedom with the certainty and unchangeableness of God's decrees about human acts, the one that has spread most widely is so-called conditional knowledge. The Jesuits Luis de Molina and Fonseca were the first to hold that the key to this reconciliation must be sought there. Very many have followed them since, both in the Roman school and among the Protestants themselves.

So, God willing, as we take up the agreement of human freedom with the divine decrees and set out the various views of the teachers on the question, we have thought it right to begin with this knowledge.

sections.title: Most Roman doctors hold that God knows not only what will be, but what would freely happen under any condition
sections.pass_a: II. Therefore the greatest part of the Doctors of the Roman School is of this opinion, that God not only foreknows those things which are freely and contingently indeed, but yet simply and absolutely future; but also those things which, although they will never be future, would yet come to pass freely, this or that condition being posited. For example, that God knows not only what each of us will do to the very end of life, in those various states in which, by the certain Providence of God, we are to be placed; but besides what we would do, if the state of things to come were plainly different, and other and other occasions of acting offered themselves to us.
pass_b: Most of the teachers of the Roman school hold that God foreknows not only what will happen freely and contingently, yet simply and absolutely. He also foreknows what will never actually happen but would happen freely if this or that condition were in place.

For example, God knows not only what each of us will do right up to the end of life in the various states in which his sure providence is to place us. He also knows what we would do if the future state of things were entirely different and other opportunities for action kept presenting themselves to us.

sections.title: This knowledge of what would be is placed before every free decree of God's will
sections.pass_a: III. Further, since the foreknowledge of those things which are absolutely future necessarily follows some decree of the divine will, by which he has determined to create these and those agents, and to set them in this, or that order of things, and to concur with them, as is necessary, for acting; they will that this knowledge of those things which are not simply future, but would be future by hypothesis only, precedes in God every free decree of the will. That is, according to our mode of conceiving, that God, before he made any decree concerning anything whatever, knew certainly and distinctly what any possible creature would do freely, if God should will to create it, and not deny it his concurrence, and propose to it these and those objects, under these and those circumstances.
pass_b: Foreknowledge of what will absolutely happen must follow some decree of God's will. By that decree he has resolved to create these or those agents, to place them in this or that order of things, and to concur with them in acting as needed.

By contrast, they hold that God's knowledge of things that will not simply happen, but would happen only on some supposition, comes before every free decree of his will. That is, to speak in our human way of conceiving, before God made any decree about anything at all, he knew with certainty and distinctness what any possible creature would freely do. He knew this on the supposition that he chose to create it, not to withhold his concurrence from it, and to set these or those objects before it in these or those circumstances.

sections.title: Yet a decree is included in the condition: not one already made, but one supposed to be made
sections.pass_a: IV. But although that knowledge antecedes any free decree in God; nevertheless, as is clear from what has been said, in the condition under which a thing is said to be future, a decree is included, not indeed one which is conceived to be actually in God, but which would necessarily have to be posited in God to this end, that that thing could be. And therefore that conditional futurition, which is the object of this knowledge, does not cease to depend on some decree of God: But not on a decree already made, but which is supposed to be made by God, that that thing can truly be called future. Namely in our manner God is conceived as thus thinking with himself, If I should decree to create this Angel, or man, and not to withdraw my concurrence from him, in such a disposition of things he would do this, and not another thing; although he could act otherwise.
pass_b: This knowledge comes before any free decree in God. Even so, as is clear from what has been said, the condition under which something is said to be future includes a decree. It is not a decree conceived as actually present in God, but one that would necessarily have to be posited in God for that thing to be able to exist.

So the conditional futurity that is the object of this knowledge still depends on a decree of God. It does not depend on a decree already made, but on one supposed to be made by God, so that the thing can truly be called future. In our human way, God is imagined reasoning with himself: 'If I decreed to create this angel or this man and not to withdraw my concurrence from him, in such an arrangement of things he would do this and nothing else, though he could act otherwise.'

sections.title: The decree on which futurity depends is not a predetermining one, but only a decree to supply concurrence
sections.pass_a: VII. However just as they do not think it necessary, that free causes may act in time, that they be premoved by God, and predetermined to this or that act: so too the decree of God on which the futurition of free acts, whether absolute, or conditional, depends, they do not think is some decree of premoving, and predetermining free causes; but that without such a decree, either simply posited, or at least supposed, God certainly foreknows whatever free agents will do either absolutely, or under a condition. That is, for this, that a thing be and be foreseen as future, it suffices if we posit, or suppose in God a decree concerning supplying concurrence, which alone they think necessary for acting, and which is such in their mind, that it is always at hand to free agents, and neither applies them to acting, nor predetermines them.
pass_b: They do not think that free causes, in order to act in time, must be premoved and predetermined by God to this or that act. In the same way, they do not think the decree of God on which the futurity of free acts depends, whether absolute or conditional, is a decree to premove and predetermine free causes.

Rather, they hold that without any such decree, whether simply laid down or at least supposed, God foreknows with certainty whatever free agents will do, absolutely or under a condition. For a thing to exist and be foreseen as future, they say, it is enough that we posit or suppose in God a decree to supply concurrence. They hold that concurrence alone is necessary for acting. As they conceive it, it is always available to free agents and neither applies them to act nor predetermines them.

sections.title: Why 'middle': between knowledge of vision (free, after the decree) and knowledge of simple intelligence
sections.pass_a: VIII. Further they call this knowledge Middle knowledge, because, according to them, it holds the middle between the knowledge which is called in the Schools knowledge of Vision, and that which is called of simple intelligence. But by knowledge of vision they understand that knowledge by which God knows those things which exist outside himself in some difference of time, namely which are past, present, or future. All which God knows from eternity as clearly, certainly, and distinctly, as if they were actually present to him, not otherwise than those things which we behold before us. Whence it is that it is called knowledge of Vision, by likeness, namely, to bodily Sight, by which we discern things set before the eyes. And this knowledge is also called free knowledge, because it follows the free decree of the divine will concerning creating and preserving things, without which, as nothing can exist, so also nothing can be seen present, or foreseen future. And so, if God had decreed to create nothing, knowledge of this kind could not be attributed to God.
pass_b: They call this knowledge 'middle knowledge' because, as they see it, it stands midway between what the schools call the knowledge of vision and the knowledge of simple intelligence.

By the knowledge of vision they mean the knowledge by which God knows things that exist outside himself at some point in time, whether past, present or future. God knows all these from eternity as clearly, certainly and distinctly as if they were actually present to him, just as we know things we see in front of us. That is why it is called the knowledge of vision, by comparison with bodily sight, by which we see things placed before our eyes.

This knowledge is also called free knowledge, because it follows the free decree of God's will to create and preserve things. Without that decree nothing can exist, and so nothing can be seen as present or foreseen as future. Had God decreed to create nothing, knowledge of this kind could not be ascribed to him.

But by knowledge of simple intelligence they signify that by which God knows and understands all possibles and the essences of things and all connexions, whether necessary, or possible in any way whatever. And this knowledge is called natural, not free; because it precedes, according to our mode of conceiving, every decree of God concerning things to be made: nor could it not be in God, although he had willed to create nothing outside himself.
pass_b: By the knowledge of simple intelligence they mean the knowledge by which God knows and understands everything possible, the essences of things, and all their connections, whether necessary or possible in any way at all.

This knowledge is called natural rather than free. In our way of conceiving, it comes before every decree of God about the things to be made. It could not have been absent from God even if he had willed to create nothing outside himself.

sections.title: Middle knowledge shares in both: free in its objects, natural in preceding every decree
sections.pass_a: X. But the knowledge which they attribute to God of things contingently future under some condition, is called middle by them, because it neither wholly agrees with the knowledge of vision, nor yet, with the knowledge of simple intelligence, but participates something of both. For neither is it of things merely possible, and abstracted from all consideration of existence, such as is the knowledge of simple intelligence: nor yet is it of things absolutely future in some difference of time, from the decree of God; such as is the knowledge of Vision: But partly it resembles free knowledge, because it is of things freely future, if only the condition were posited, and it is placed in the liberty of God, that that condition be posited: partly natural knowledge, because it precedes every decree of God, and God could not lack it, even if he had not decreed the world, or to create anything.
pass_b: They call God's knowledge of things that would happen contingently under some condition 'middle' because it neither fully matches the knowledge of vision nor the knowledge of simple intelligence, but shares something of each.

It is not about merely possible things considered apart from any question of existence, as the knowledge of simple intelligence is. Nor is it about things that will absolutely happen at some point in time by God's decree, as the knowledge of vision is.

In part it resembles free knowledge, because it concerns things that would happen freely if only the condition were met, and whether the condition is met lies in God's freedom. In part it resembles natural knowledge, because it comes before every decree of God, and God could not have been without it even if he had not decreed the world or decreed to create anything.

Vasquez does note, though, that nothing prevents setting up some third category between those two kinds of divine knowledge for the sake of teaching and clarity. sections.title: Scripture proof: David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23) — God foreknew what Saul and the Keilites would do
sections.pass_a: XII. However that such knowledge belongs to God, by which he certainly foreknows things contingently future under some condition, they think can be proved by testimonies of Scripture, and arguments drawn from reason. And first indeed from Scripture they bring forward various examples of predictions concerning those things which did not indeed happen, but which, these or those things being posited, were going to come to pass: Such is that which is read 1 Sam. 23, v. 11, 12. Where when David had asked the Lord, Whether if he remained in the City Keilah, Saul would come to take him. And if he came, Whether the Keilites would deliver him into the hand of Saul? he received answer both that Saul would come, and that the Keilites would deliver him into the hand of Saul, if he remained in the city Keilah. And therefore each of those things, which depended on the free will of Saul and of the Keilites, God certainly foreknew, under a condition which did not take place, David taking to flight, for which cause neither was actually done.
pass_b: They think it can be proved, both from the testimony of Scripture and from arguments of reason, that God has knowledge by which he foreknows with certainty things that would happen contingently under some condition.

From Scripture they first cite various examples of predictions about things that did not actually happen but would have happened had certain things been in place. One is 1 Samuel 23:11-12. David asked the Lord whether, if he stayed in the city of Keilah, Saul would come to capture him, and whether, if Saul came, the men of Keilah would hand him over to Saul. He was told both that Saul would come and that the men of Keilah would hand him over, if he stayed in Keilah.

So God foreknew with certainty both these things, which depended on the free will of Saul and of the men of Keilah, under a condition that never came about. David fled, and for that reason neither thing actually happened.

sections.title: Argument from reason: conditional propositions about future contingents are determinately true or false
sections.pass_a: XV. Moreover they think it can be proved by many arguments drawn from reason that such knowledge is found in God. And first indeed from this, that in propositions concerning a future contingent under some condition there is determinate truth, or falsity, no less than in propositions concerning those things which are absolutely future; and therefore those too are the object of divine knowledge: since no truth can lie hidden from an infinite intellect, such as the divine is. But that propositions concerning future contingents under some condition are determinately true, or false, is concluded from this that between them there can be true contradiction, no otherwise than between those which are about things absolutely future. Since these plainly contradict each other, If Peter be placed in such circumstances, he will sin, And, Not if Peter be placed in such circumstances, will he sin. But in all contradictories, it is necessary that one part of the contradiction be true, the other false.
pass_b: They also think many arguments from reason prove that God has such knowledge. The first is this. Propositions about a future contingent under some condition have determinate truth or falsity, just as much as propositions about things that will absolutely happen. So they too are objects of God's knowledge, since no truth can be hidden from an infinite intellect, which the divine intellect is.

That propositions about future contingents under a condition are determinately true or false follows from the fact that there can be genuine contradiction between them, just as between propositions about things that will absolutely happen. These two plainly contradict each other: 'If Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin' and 'It is not the case that if Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin.' In every pair of contradictories one side must be true and the other false.

sections.title: A wise agent foresees consequences before deciding; so God knew what creatures would do before decreeing

sections.title: Without it, endless questions would have no answer from God, or would need infinite idle decrees
sections.pass_a: XVIII. Add that, unless we attribute such knowledge to God, infinite questions could be proposed to God, after the manner of those which David proposed, to which God could answer nothing certain and clear, except that it is a thing which cannot be known; which seems to detract not a little from all divine knowledge. For example, let someone ask, what that man would have done, who died a peaceful death in Christ, if martyrdom had been offered to him? Whether if this, or that man had sought marriage with such a girl, who married another, before him, he would have obtained consent or not? if a certain person were elected king of Poland, how he would conduct himself in that kingdom? and infinite things of this kind, concerning which since sagacious men, and men experienced in affairs can make conjectures, it is not likely that they are simply unknown to God. And it seems unworthy of God, that he should not have ascertained certainly, what a man can attain by probable conjecture. But if anyone say, that God knows such things indeed, and can answer distinctly and clearly concerning them, but that such knowledge presupposes a free decree concerning the futurition of those things, in this or that case, thence it will follow that there are in God infinite decrees concerning things never actually future, and therefore vain, empty, and idle which is very absurd.
pass_b: Besides, unless we ascribe such knowledge to God, countless questions could be put to him, like the ones David asked, to which God could give no certain and clear answer except that the matter cannot be known. That seems to take a good deal away from God's omniscience.

Suppose someone asks what a man who died peacefully in Christ would have done if martyrdom had been offered him. Or whether this or that man, had he sought the hand of a certain girl before the man she married, would have won her consent or not. Or how a certain person would conduct himself if he were elected king of Poland. There are endless questions of this kind.

Shrewd and experienced people can make guesses about such things, so it is unlikely that God is simply ignorant of them. It seems unworthy of God not to know for certain what a man can reach by probable conjecture.

Someone may say that God does know such things and can answer distinctly and clearly about them, but that such knowledge presupposes a free decree about whether those things would come about in this or that case. Then it will follow that there are in God countless decrees about things that will never actually happen. Those decrees would be pointless, empty and idle, which is quite absurd.

sections.title: Their reason: nothing is future, absolutely or conditionally, except by a decree predetermining the will
sections.pass_a: XX. For they think that nothing is in any way future, either absolutely, or under a condition, except by virtue of some decree, which actually precedes in God, and by which God has determined either to effect, or at least to permit that which is said to be future; and so before the decree of the divine will predetermining the will to one part of a contradiction, or of a contrariety, it is not knowable what in particular a man will do, or what he would do, if he were placed in such circumstances; but only what he could do: and that because before such a decree, the thing is neither future, nor not future, but merely possible, and indifferent to this, that it be future, or not be future.
pass_b: In their view, nothing becomes future, whether outright or on a condition, unless a decree actually comes first in God and gives it that status. Through such a decree God settles that what is called future will be brought about by him, or at the least allowed.

It follows that, until God's will has decreed to predetermine the human will toward one of two contradictory or contrary options, no one can know what a particular person will do. Nor can anyone know what he would do in such circumstances; all that can be known is what he is able to do. Before such a decree the thing is not yet future and not yet non-future. It is simply possible, and open either way.

sections.title: They grant conditional predictions (Keilah) but make them follow a decree to permit and predetermine (Alvarez)
sections.pass_a: XXI. Therefore they do not indeed deny that certain things contingently and freely future under some condition are certainly foreknown by God, and foretold in Scripture, as God foretold to David, that if he remained in the city Keilah Saul was going to come to seize him; and again that, if Saul came to that city, the inhabitants were going to deliver him into the hands of Saul: But they contend that that certain foreknowledge of God follows a free decree in God, by which he determined that these or those things should be done, if this or that condition be fulfilled. For example, that God foreknew that, David remaining in the city Keilah, Saul would come, and the Keilites would deliver David, because, that condition being posited, God had decreed both to permit, and to predetermine to the substance of those acts the will of Saul, and of the inhabitants of the city Keilah. As may be seen more at large in Didacus Alvarez on the Aids of divine grace book 1, chapter 6, whose Title is, That besides merely natural knowledge, and merely free, no middle knowledge is to be constituted, even in God. And in the following chapter also, in which he dissolves the objections of the Doctors of the different opinion.
pass_b: They do not deny that some things that would happen contingently and freely under a condition are foreknown by God with certainty and foretold in Scripture. God foretold to David that if he stayed in Keilah, Saul would come to seize him, and that if Saul came to that city, its inhabitants would hand David over to him.

But they insist that this certain foreknowledge of God follows a free decree in God, by which he determined that this or that should happen if this or that condition were fulfilled. Thus God foreknew that if David stayed in Keilah, Saul would come and the people of Keilah would hand David over. He foreknew it because, given that condition, he had decreed both to permit those acts and to predetermine to their substance the wills of Saul and of the inhabitants of Keilah.

This can be seen at greater length in Didacus Alvarez, On the Aids of Divine Grace, book 1, chapter 6, titled 'That besides merely natural and merely free knowledge, no middle knowledge is to be posited, even in God.' sections.title: Episcopius on the threefold knowledge, approving the distinction as useful for teaching
sections.pass_a: XXIII. And first indeed Simon Episcopius reports as convenient the distinction of a threefold knowledge in God, solemn from the times of Molina. It comes to be observed, he says, that a threefold knowledge is wont to be attributed to God. One, which is necessary, and practical, and is called of simple intelligence, which from its nature is prior to every act of the free will, by which God understands himself and all other possible things. Another free, which is called of Vision, and is posterior to the act of the free Will, by which God knows all things, which he has decreed to do, or permit in the same order in which he decreed to do them, or to permit that they be done. A Third Middle, by which God knows what men, or Angels would do according to their liberty, under a condition, if they were set with these or those circumstances, in this or in that state, or order. Whether this distinction of the divine knowledge be rightly made, we do not weigh. That it can be made conveniently and for the sake of teaching, we by no means doubt. Of the Theological Institutions book four, chapter 19, On the order and mode of the divine knowledge.
pass_b: First, Simon Episcopius reports with approval the threefold distinction of knowledge in God that has been standard since Molina. 'It should be noted,' he says, 'that a threefold knowledge is usually ascribed to God.

One is necessary and practical and is called the knowledge of simple intelligence. By its nature it comes before every act of the free will, and by it God understands himself and everything else that is possible.

The second is free and is called the knowledge of vision. It comes after the act of the free will, and by it God knows everything he has decreed to do or permit, in the same order in which he decreed to do it or permit it to happen.
The third is middle knowledge, by which God knows what men or angels would do in their freedom under a condition, if they were placed in these or those circumstances, in this or that state or order.

Whether this distinction of divine knowledge is correctly drawn we do not examine. That it can be drawn usefully and for the sake of teaching we do not doubt at all.' Theological Institutions, book 4, chapter 19, On the order and manner of divine knowledge.

sections.pass_a: XXV. But also among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some are found acknowledging in God that conditional knowledge, by which before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause, in any order of things, according to the liberty inborn in it, would do. Among whom first that Franciscus Gomarus seems to be numbered, already cited by Curcellaeus for this opinion. For writing on the place Matt. 11, v. 21. After he observed that the Penitence of the Tyrians, the condition of Christ's miracles being posited, future, is understood to be of this kind, which is common to the Elect and Reprobate, to believers and unbelievers: such, in his mind, was the Penitence of the Ninevites with sackcloth; he subjoins these very words, But what Christ asserts of this future penitence of the Tyrians, that condition being posited, its truth stands firm from the indefinite foreknowledge of his divine nature, by which he knows what, an antecedent being posited, would have followed, even if neither came to pass. For that condition being posited, that one or the other would have come to pass, that they either would do penitence, or would not, is known to all from that principle, that two opposites cannot be true at once: but which of them would have been future, since the thing was contingent, he alone foresaw, who sees all things by his infinite knowledge, and certainly foretells not only necessary things, but also future contingents. A similar place is Ezek. 3, v. 6, 7. As Baldvinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament at the place of Matthew cited.
pass_b: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some acknowledge in God this conditional knowledge, by which, before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause would do in any order of things, according to its innate freedom. Commenting on Matthew 11:21, Gomarus first notes that the repentance of Tyre that would have followed Christ's miracles is to be understood as the kind common to elect and reprobate, believers and unbelievers. 'What Christ asserts about this repentance of Tyre that would have followed under that condition is true by virtue of the unbounded foreknowledge of his divine nature. By it he knows what would have followed given an antecedent, even if neither came about. Given that condition, everyone knows that one or the other would have happened, that they would either repent or not, from the principle that two opposites cannot both be true at once. But which of them would have happened, since the matter was contingent, only he foresaw who sees all things by his infinite knowledge and foretells with certainty not only necessary things but future contingents too. So Balduinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament, at the passage of Matthew cited.

sections.title: Antonius Walaeus admits middle knowledge, proving it from Matthew 24 (days shortened; the elect not deceived)

But especially Antonius Walaeus Professor in the Academy of Leiden acknowledges in God middle knowledge, by which from hypothesis things future are known, although they are not absolutely future, or are not yet. He holds, for example, that God foreknew that Adam would misuse his freedom if God made him such as he was, endowed him with such gifts, allowed him to be tempted, and so on. The same holds, he thinks, for the other outcomes of free choice that depend on the choice of angels or human beings.

pass_b: Paul Ferry, the celebrated minister of God's Word at Metz, also admits in God this conditional knowledge of future things, which comes before the free decree. 'By what they call his conditional knowledge,' he says, 'God foreknew that man would do this or that, in whatever way he made him. So he foreknew that man would fall if God created him able to fall, allowed him to be tempted, and left him to himself, given his innate freedom to go either way and the weakness of a creature.
If man fell, God foreknew that all would perish, if he so willed; or he could rescue some from it, so as to display his justice in the one group and his grace in the other,' and so on.

Later, setting out the reasoning of God's providence regarding the fall, he says: 'First, God foresaw that man would fall if he were created able to fall and were tempted. Next, because he saw that it was fitting, it pleased him that this should happen. He did not force man, but created him that way and left him to temptation and to himself.'

A little further on he adds that God determined nothing about man's fall without first foreseeing that, given freedom and temptation, man would infallibly fall. Vindiciae pro Scholastico Orthodoxo, pages 203, 209 and 210.

sections.title: Many Reformed reject it: God knows conditional truths, but from his free decree, not before it
sections.pass_a: XXXII. But many other Theologians of the Reformed reject that Middle and conditional knowledge in God as vain and superfluous: not all however in the same mode, nor resting on the same foundations. And first indeed there are some who grant that all propositions which deny or affirm something contingently future, under whatever condition, are determinately true or false, and therefore also knowable by God; for neither is it doubtful to anyone that God certainly knows and apprehends every truth. And so they affirm that there is no question concerning free and conditional futures, imaginable by human or angelic intellect, to which God cannot clearly answer, this or that condition being posited, that the thing will so be. Yet they deny that it follows thence that there is any conditional knowledge in God, which antecedes the free decree of God. And that because God knows those things indeed, but from the free decree of his will, by which he predefined with himself from eternity not only the modes and connexions of things future in time, but also of things never future, and only possible to be done; but with this difference, that he willed the former to be done, the latter he did not will: which yet if he willed, would be future just as he had predefined. Which are the words of Matthias Nethenus in Gisbertus Voetius, a most Celebrated man, and with the same Voetius approving, in the first part of the Theological Disputations, in the theses on conditional or Middle knowledge in God, section three, num. 18.
pass_b: Many other Reformed theologians, however, reject this middle and conditional knowledge in God as empty and superfluous. They do not all do so in the same way, though, or rely on the same grounds.

First, some grant that every proposition denying or affirming that something will happen contingently, under any condition, is determinately true or false, and so knowable by God. No one doubts that God knows and grasps every truth with certainty. So they affirm that no question about free and conditional future things that a human or angelic mind can imagine is one God cannot answer clearly: given this or that condition, the matter will turn out thus.

Yet they deny that it follows that God has any conditional knowledge preceding his free decree. God does know these things, but from the free decree of his will. By that decree he predefined with himself from eternity the modes and connections not only of things that will happen in time but also of things that never will and are merely possible. There is this difference: the former he willed to happen, the latter he did not. Yet if he had willed them, they would happen just as he had predefined.

These are the words of Matthias Nethenus, given in the work of the celebrated Gisbertus Voetius and approved by Voetius himself: Theological Disputations, part 1, theses on conditional or middle knowledge in God, section 3, number 18.
